questions.problem: The acceleration of a cyclist is $1.5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ What is the cyclist's acceleration in ${\text{km/s}}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}},$ and we want to convert this into $\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.$ To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

$$
\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}
$$

We want to replace $\text{m}$ with $\text{km}.$ To get rid of $\text{m},$ we can put $\text{m}$ in the denominator so that it cancels out. To introduce $\text{km},$ we can put $\text{km}$ in the numerator.

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{m}}}=\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\text{m}}=\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The acceleration given in the problem statement is $1.5\,\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.$

- There are $1\,000$ meters per kilometer. Taking the reciprocal, there are $\frac{1}{1\,000}$ kilometers per meter.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}1.5\,\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}} & =1.5\,\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{1\,000}\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{m}} \\  & =1.5\cdot \frac{1}{1\,000}(\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{m}}}) \\  & =0.001\,5\,\frac{\text{km}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the acceleration of the cyclist is $0.001\,5\,\text{km}/{\text{s}}^{2}.$

questions.problem: A cruise ship on the high seas travels at a speed of $972$ centimeters per second. What is the speed of the ship in meters per second?
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{s}},$ and we want to convert this into $\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}.$ To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

$$
\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{s}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}
$$

We want to replace $\text{cm}$ with $\text{m}.$ To get rid of $\text{cm},$ we can put $\text{cm}$ in the denominator so that it cancels out. To introduce $\text{m},$ we can put $\text{m}$ in the numerator.

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{cm}}}{\text{s}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{cm}}}=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{s}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\text{cm}}=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The speed given in the problem statement is $972\,\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{s}}.$

- There are $100$ centimeters per meter. Taking the reciprocal, there are $\frac{1}{100}$ meters per centimeter.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}972\,\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{s}} & =972\,\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{s}}\cdot \frac{1}{100}\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{cm}} \\  & =972\cdot \frac{1}{100}(\frac{\cancel{\text{cm}}}{\text{s}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{cm}}}) \\  & =9.72\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the speed of the cruise is $9.72\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

questions.problem: A car travels at a speed of $2.5$ kilometers per minute. What is this in kilometers per hour?
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\frac{\text{km}}{\text{min}},$ and we want to convert this into $\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}.$ To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

$$
\frac{\text{km}}{\text{min}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}
$$

We want to replace $\text{min}$ with $\text{hour}.$ To get rid of $\text{min},$ we can put $\text{min}$ in the numerator so that it cancels out. To introduce $\text{hour},$ we can put $\text{hour}$ in the denominator.

$$
\frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{min}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{min}}}{\text{hour}}=\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\frac{\text{km}}{\text{min}}\cdot \frac{\text{min}}{\text{hour}}=\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The rate given in the problem statement is $2.5\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{min}}.$

- There are $60$ minutes in one hour.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2.5\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{min}} & =2.5\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{min}}\cdot 60\,\frac{\text{min}}{\text{hour}} \\  & =2.5\cdot 60(\frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{min}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{min}}}{\text{hour}}) \\  & =150\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A tree sapling grows by $2$ centimeters per day. Assuming that one year has $365$ days, how many meters does the tree grow in one year?
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{day}},$ and we want to convert this into $\frac{\text{m}}{\text{year}}.$ We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

$$
\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{day}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{year}}
$$

One of the conversion factors should change $\text{cm}$ to $\text{m}.$

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{cm}}}{\text{day}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{cm}}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{year}}
$$

The other conversion factor should change $\text{day}$ into $\text{year}.$

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{cm}}}{\cancel{\text{day}}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{cm}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{days}}}{\text{year}}=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{year}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{day}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\text{cm}}\cdot \frac{\text{days}}{\text{year}}=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{year}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The rate given in the problem statement is $2\,\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{day}}.$

- There are $100$ centimeters in one meter, therefore, there are $\frac{1}{100}$ meters in one centimeter.

- There are $365$ days in one year.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\,\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{day}} & =2\,\frac{\text{cm}}{\text{day}}\cdot \frac{1}{100}\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{cm}}\cdot 365\,\frac{\text{days}}{\text{year}} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{100}\cdot 365(\frac{\cancel{\text{cm}}}{\cancel{\text{day}}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{cm}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{days}}}{\text{year}}) \\  & =7.3\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{year}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $2$ centimeters per day is equivalent to $7.3$ meters per year. In one year, the tree grows by $7.3$ meters.

questions.problem: Lewis spends $0.5$ hours per day studying. How many minutes per week does Lewis study for?
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\frac{\text{hours}}{\text{day}},$ and we want to convert this into $\frac{\text{min}}{\text{week}}.$ We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

$$
\frac{\text{hours}}{\text{day}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{min}}{\text{week}}
$$

One of the conversion factors should change $\text{hours}$ to $\text{min}.$

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{hours}}}{\text{day}}\cdot \frac{\text{min}}{\cancel{\text{hour}}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}
$$

The other conversion factor should change $\text{day}$ into $\text{week}.$

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{hours}}}{\cancel{\text{day}}}\cdot \frac{\text{min}}{\cancel{\text{hour}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{days}}}{\text{week}}=\frac{\text{min}}{\text{week}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\frac{\text{hours}}{\text{day}}\cdot \frac{\text{min}}{\text{hour}}\cdot \frac{\text{days}}{\text{week}}=\frac{\text{min}}{\text{week}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The rate given in the problem statement is $0.5\,\frac{\text{hours}}{\text{day}}.$

- There are $60$ minutes per hour.

- There are $7$ days per week.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.5\,\frac{\text{hours}}{\text{day}} & =0.5\,\frac{\text{hours}}{\text{day}}\cdot 60\,\frac{\text{min}}{\text{hour}}\cdot 7\,\frac{\text{days}}{\text{week}} \\  & =(0.5\cdot 60\cdot 7)\,\frac{\cancel{\text{hours}}}{\cancel{\text{day}}}\cdot \frac{\text{min}}{\cancel{\text{hour}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{days}}}{\text{week}} \\  & =210\,\frac{\text{min}}{\text{week}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, Lewis studies at a rate of $210\,\text{min/week}.$

canonical_examples.problem: A guitar string, made of carbon steel, has a linear mass density of $3\,950$ milligrams per meter. What is the linear mass density in grams per meter?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}},$ and we want to convert this into $\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}.$ To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}
$$

We want to replace $\textrm{mg}$ with $\textrm{g}.$ To get rid of $\textrm{mg},$ we can put $\textrm{mg}$ in the denominator so that it cancels out. To introduce $\textrm{g},$ we can put $\textrm{g}$ in the numerator.

$$
\require{cancel}
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{mg}} }{\textrm{m}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{g} }{\cancel{ \textrm{mg} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\require{cancel}
\dfrac{\textrm{mg} }{\textrm{m}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{g} }{ \textrm{mg} } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The density given in the problem statement is $3\,950 \, \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}.$

- There are $1\,000$ milligrams per gram. Taking the reciprocal, there are $\dfrac{1}{1\,000}$ grams per milligram.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3\,950\,\frac{\text{mg}}{\text{m}} & =3\,950\,\frac{\text{mg}}{\text{m}}\cdot \frac{1}{1\,000}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mg}} \\  & =(3\,950\cdot \frac{1}{1\,000})\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mg}}}{\text{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mg}}} \\  & =3.95\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{m}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the linear mass density of the string is $3.95\,\textrm{g}/\textrm{m}.$

canonical_examples.problem: Sand runs through a sand timer at a rate of $120$ grams per minute. What is this rate in grams per second?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{min}},$ and we want to convert this into $\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}.$ To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{min}}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

We want to replace $\textrm{min}$ with $\textrm{s}.$ To get rid of $\textrm{min},$ we can put $\textrm{min}$ in the numerator so that it cancels out. To introduce $\textrm{s},$ we can put $\textrm{s}$ in the denominator.

$$
\require{cancel}
\dfrac{\textrm{g} }{ \cancel{\textrm{min}}}\cdot \dfrac{ \cancel{ \textrm{min} } }{ \textrm{s} } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

Therefore, our conversion formula is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{g} }{ \textrm{min}}\cdot \dfrac{  \textrm{min}  }{ \textrm{s} } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The rate given in the problem statement is $120 \, \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{min}}.$

- There are $60$ seconds per minute. Taking the reciprocal, there are $\dfrac{1}{60}$ minutes per second.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}120\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}} & =120\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}\cdot \frac{1}{60}\,\frac{\text{min}}{\text{s}} \\  & =(120\cdot \frac{1}{60})\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{min}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{min}}}{\text{s}} \\  & =2\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the sand runs through the sand timer at a rate of $2 \,\textrm{g}/\textrm{s}.$

canonical_examples.problem: A peregrine falcon can reach a speed of $360$ kilometers per hour during flight while diving. What is this speed in meters per second?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We are given the units $\dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{hour}},$ and we want to convert this into $\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}.$ We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{hour}}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

One of the conversion factors should change $\textrm{km}$ to $\textrm{m}.$

$$
\dfrac{\cancel{\color{blue}\textrm{km}} }{\textrm{hour}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\cancel{\color{blue}\textrm{km}} } \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

The other conversion factor should change $\textrm{hour}$ into $\textrm{s}.$

$$
\dfrac{\cancel{\color{blue}\textrm{km}} }{ \cancel{\color{red}\textrm{hour}} }\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\cancel{\color{blue}\textrm{km}} } \cdot \dfrac{ \cancel{\color{red}\textrm{hour}} }{ \textrm{s} } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\dfrac{\color{black}\textrm{km} }{ \color{black}\textrm{hour} }\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\color{black}\textrm{km} } \cdot \dfrac{ \color{black}\textrm{hour} }{ \textrm{s} } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The rate given in the problem statement is $360 \, \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{hour}}.$

- There are $1\,000$ meters per kilometer.

- The number of seconds in one hour is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1\,\text{hour} & =60\,\text{minutes} \\  & =60\cdot 1\,\text{minute} \\  & =60\cdot 60\,\text{s} \\  & =3\,600\,\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are $\dfrac{1}{3\,600}$ hours per second.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}360\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}} & =360\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}\cdot 1\,000\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{km}}\cdot \frac{1}{3\,600}\,\frac{\text{hour}}{\text{s}} \\  & =(360\cdot 1\,000\cdot \frac{1}{3\,600})\,\frac{\cancel{\text{km}}}{\cancel{\text{hour}}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{km}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{hour}}}{\text{s}} \\  & =100\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the speed of the falcon is $100$ meters per second.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We can use unit conversions to convert from one set of units to another.

For instance, the speed of sound is approximately $0.34$ kilometers per second. What is this in meters per second? We can find out using the following two steps.

** Step 1: Create a conversion formula.**

We are given the units $\dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{s}},$ and we want to convert this into $\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}.$ To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{km}}{s}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

We want to replace $\textrm{km}$ with $\textrm{m}.$ To get rid of $\textrm{km},$ we can put $\textrm{km}$ in the denominator so that it cancels out:

$$
\require{cancel}
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}} }{s}\cdot \dfrac{?}{\cancel{ \textrm{km} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

Then, to introduce $\textrm{m},$ we can put $\textrm{m}$ in the numerator:

$$
\require{cancel}
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}} }{s}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m} }{\cancel{ \textrm{km} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{km}}{s}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m} }{\textrm{km} } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}.
$$

**Step 2: Use the conversion formula.**

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The speed that we wish to convert is $0.34 \, \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{s}}.$

- There are $1\,000$ meters per kilometer.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.34\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{s}} & =0.34\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{s}}\cdot 1\,000\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{km}} \\  & =(0.34\cdot 1\,000)\,\frac{\cancel{\text{km}}}{\text{s}}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{km}}} \\  & =340\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the speed of sound is $340$ meters per second.
